passage: The dairy society office in the kasba smelled of milk cans and damp registers. Jyoti had been there four months, and Farooq had been kind since the first week. He had found her a room and shown her the shortcut to the bus stand. So when she saw him shaving a little off the weights in the morning register, she stared at the page for a long time. Her chest felt tight. That evening she waited by the tea stall. "Farooq bhai, the entries don't match the scale. You need to fix them." He laughed, then looked away. "Everyone does it, it's small." "It's not small if it's the farmers' milk," she said, her voice shaking. "You have until Friday. After that I will have to tell the secretary." He said nothing, and she walked home wondering if she'd lost a friend.

qa.q: How long had Jyoti been at the dairy society office?
qa.a: Jyoti had been there four months.

qa.q: What was Jyoti feeling when she saw Farooq shaving the weights?
qa.a: Torn and tense: her chest felt tight, she stared at the page a long time, and she wondered if she had lost a friend.

qa.q: What did Jyoti do that balanced loyalty and honesty?
qa.a: She spoke to Farooq privately, asked him to fix the entries by Friday and said she would tell the secretary afterwards.

qa.q: How might Farooq have felt hearing Jyoti's words at the tea stall?
qa.a: Probably embarrassed and defensive, since he laughed, looked away and said everyone does it.

grounding: The wrongdoer is a friend who helped her settle in; she feels torn, gives him a chance to correct it, and sets a limit on silence.

passage:
Tejas, you look like someone carrying a stone. Is it about your colleague? Then let your Irawati bua tell you something. When I was twenty-two, at the bank in Jabalpur, the man who taught me everything was Prakash. He found me a room, showed me the ledgers, shared his lunch when my salary was late.

One evening I saw him quietly move money from an old widow's dormant account into a suspense entry. Once, then again the next month.

I felt sick, and torn. He had been so good to me. So I went to him first, alone. "Prakash ji, I saw the entries. Please put it right, and tell the manager yourself. I'll wait till Friday."

He begged, then went silent. Friday came and nothing changed. On Monday I went to the branch manager with the dates. It cost me his friendship. But I slept again.

qa.q: Whose account did Prakash move money from?
qa.a: He moved money from an old widow's dormant account.

qa.q: How did young Irawati feel when she saw the entries?
qa.a: Young Irawati felt sick and torn, because the man doing wrong had been so good to her.

qa.q: What turning point in the story shows loyalty and truth together?
qa.a: Irawati gave Prakash a chance to correct it by Friday, and when he didn't, she reported it to the manager on Monday.

qa.q: How might Prakash have felt when Irawati confronted him?
qa.a: Prakash likely felt frightened and ashamed, begging and then going silent.

grounding: The elder's story shows a young woman whose wrongdoing colleague was a friend who helped her settle in, giving him a chance to correct it but not staying silent.

passage:
The audit was next Wednesday, and Akash knew exactly what the auditors would find. At the pharma warehouse in Baddi, the fridge temperature logs for the vaccine room had been filled in neatly, every two hours, for three weeks, while the fridge was broken. Sumit had written them. Sumit, who had picked Akash up from the bus stand on his first day and found him a room.

Akash spent two nights barely sleeping. On Friday he caught Sumit alone in the loading bay. "I know about the logs. You have to tell Minakshi ma'am before Monday. Those vaccines could be useless."

Sumit's face went white. "You'd do this to me?"

"I'm doing it for the kids who get those vaccines. Monday."

Monday came. Sumit said nothing. At noon Akash knocked on the quality manager's door. Minakshi ma'am listened, pulled the stock aside the same afternoon and called Sumit in.

qa.a: Akash caught Sumit alone in the loading bay.

qa.q: What was Akash feeling during the two sleepless nights?
qa.a: Akash felt torn and anxious, caught between loyalty to Sumit and worry about the vaccines.

qa.q: Which of Akash's choices were wise, and why?
qa.a: Giving Sumit a deadline to come forward himself, then reporting to the quality manager when he didn't, was fair to Sumit and protected the vaccines.

qa.q: How did Sumit see Akash's warning?
qa.a: Sumit saw it as betrayal at first, asking "You'd do this to me?", after all the help he had given.

grounding: The story shows a young man torn when a friend who helped him settle in has done wrong, giving him a chance to correct it and then reporting.
